messages.body_plain:
The help says that the first argument 'arglist' a "list of argument lists for secr.fit or a character vector naming such lists...". The 'dontrun' example shows the second of these forms:

messages.subject: detectors with different g0 in secrdesign
messages.subject_clean: detectors with different g0 in secrdesign
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

We are designing a hair collection study for bears. The majority of our detectors will be natural rub objects. However, there is an opportunity to have some of the more traditional lured hair snag corrals in part of the study area. I would like to use secrdesign to evaluate the effect of having two kinds of detectors with different g0 on the precision of our estimates. I would assume that g0(rub object) < g0(lured corral). I would like to get a sense of whether adding the lured corrals would improve our estimate, and if so, how many we might need to add, and where. How could I implement this in secrdesign?

I envision the data from our study could then be analyzed by including detector type as a covariate for g0.

Thank you for any suggestions!
Hannah

messages.subject_clean: detectors with different g0 in secrdesign
messages.body_plain:
I don't know if there is a straightforward way to do it. 'secrdesign' uses the 'secr' function sim.capthist to simulate detections. That allows g0 and sigma to vary by occasion, but not by detector. Which enables this ad hoc solution based on separate 'rub tree' and 'hair snag' sampling occasions:
1. construct a detector (traps) object with 'usage' attribute '1' or '0' for each detector on a particular occasion according to whether that is a rub tree or hair snag occasion
2. construct the 'det.args' argument for run.scenarios() using a detectpar with a vector of values for g0, depending on the 'occasion'.
At least, I hope that works. Some trial and error may be called for (with fit = FALSE!). For most models the sequential position of rub tree and hair snag occasions won't matter. [I prefer to describe hair snags as 'rigorous' and rub trees as 'cheap and cheerful', but maybe, just maybe, I'm prejudiced :-)]
Murray

messages.subject: Transect data
messages.body_plain:
I have a question about transect data. In the online and workshop
materials I could find they are treated somewhat parenthetically so I want to make
sure I understand the data input correctly.

If I missed some materials that explain this approach, I'd appreciate a push in the right direction.

First, the transects are entered as a series of x-y coordinates similar
to the vertices of a polygon detector, correct?

If so, here are my questions:

1. Murray (2013) makes a statement in Appendix D that transects
cannot loop back on themselves. I'm not exactly clear on the limitations
of transect layout We had field techs generally follow a rectangle
transect (to end up at their start point - logistically efficient) and
record a tracklog of their path. However, that was a general guideline
because we needed them to search for quality scat samples (for DNA) so I
allowed them to deviate as they thought appropriate. Do I need to
simplify this path into a series of straight-line paths that do not
cross over themselves? Is that sufficient?

2. If I simplify the transects, I then have to make sure the locations
of where deer pellets are detected fall exactly on the transect line,
correct? In my situation, I don't think any error introduced by doing
this will affect density estimates because the individual transects are smaller
than the home range of a deer and there are multiple transects.

3. Is there another way to skin this cat? For example, could I make the
transect a series of point detectors and simply assign a scat detection
to the nearest detector? If so, any rule of thumb on distance between
detectors?  Transects are about 0.5 km long and spaced several km apart.

Thanks,

Duane

messages.subject: Re: Transect data
messages.body_plain:
On your first question, input of transect data should follow the pattern for polygon data: x-y coords of each detection are provided in columns 4,5 of the capture file and fmt = 'XY' (see secr-datainput.pdf <http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-datainput.pdf>).

My reticience about the 'transect' detector type is based on (i) never having used it in anger myself (ii) knowing that the probability model has an assumption (detection rate/probability scales with the length of transect intersecting the home range UD) that is potentially violated if the transect is wiggly, with unknown effects, and (iii) knowing that some fairly tortuous programming was involved.

I am very comfortable with your third point: modelling transect detectors as a series of point detectors. I have added a function 'discretize' for polygons in 2.10.0, and maybe should look at the same for transects.

If your individual transects are smaller than the home range of a deer, are you relying on re-detections between transects to get the home-range scale? It seems you could use quite coarse discretization within transects without losing information.

 Murray

messages.subject_clean: Want to model effect of group size on (g0)
messages.body_plain:
Hello Keshab

This is a question for which I don't know a simple answer. The main SECR models assume detections occur independently, so there is a fundamental difficulty with social animals that are sighted as a group. Distance methods switch to counting whole groups and adjusting for average group size. It is not usually possible to do this with passive detections in SECR. Although it may be technically possible if you are visually detecting groups, probably you have too few groups for this to be a sensible solution. Perhaps SECR is just not an appropriate method. I can imagine a complex hierarchical model that allowed for grouping, but I can't help any further on that.

You could go through the motions of fitting an SECR model in secr ignoring the independence question. In that case group size - if it is constant over time - is like other individual covariates: include it as an extra column in your capture file, name it with the covnames argument of read.capthist, and use the name in a formula for g0 or sigma when fitting a conditional likelihood model
CH <- read.capthist(..., covnames = 'groupsize')
fit <- secr.fit(CH, CL = TRUE, model = list(g0~groupsize))
derived(fit)
(This will take a long time to fit, especially if there are many different group sizes).

If group size varies (I assume it does) then we don't have an answer at present, but you could possibly use an average for each individual. I emphasise that I don't know of canned solutions that are proven to work for social animals, but others are working in this area.

Murray

I don't really think you have too much data, and I'm still hoping this is solvable by carefully configuring the analysis. ~t models are usually a waste of time (slow to fit because of the extra parameters, and negligible change in density estimates). I don't quite understand your layout - 130 polygons? If you are still stuck you could send me the data for one session offline and I'll take it as a challenge.
Murray

On Sat, Dec 19, 2015 at 8:21 AM, Marco Basile <marco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi secr users,
> As I said I have 383 traps and 1065 captures.
> I tried to run session (just the first session, includind 4 occasions and 313 captures) separately but, altough the null model ran in 37 minutes, just adding one covariates to D and setting g0 ~ t resulted in hours to run. I also tried grouping traps over polygon (130 polygon) and discretize function but results aren't getting better.
>
> Am I missing something, or my dataset is simply too large?
>
> Regards
> Marco
>
>
> Il 10/12/2015 19.26, Marco Basile ha scritto:
> > Thank you Murray I will let you informed
> >
> > Marco
> >
> > Il 10/12/2015 19.19, Murray Efford ha scritto:
> > > Collapsing occasions is certainly a good idea, and I'd advise you to persist with that. Using multiple cores never seems to help much in secr.fit() because of the overheads in handling the worker processes. Not sure what you mean by one mesh per trap, so mask size could still be a problem (I would aim for nrow(mask) 1000-2000. Try running sessions separately. 4Gb is not an awful lot, but I survived with that until upgrading last week.
> > > Murray
> > >
> > > On Fri, Dec 11, 2015 at 5:48 AM, Marco Basile <marco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > My traps are related to trees, of which I have variables (like diameter) to use as covariates. I have 383 trap sites and a mask with 1 mesh per trap.
> > > >
> > > > Are the traps too many, in your opinion? Anyway, I will try memory.size().
> > > >
> > > > Thanks a lot
> > > > Marco

> > > > > Hi Marco,
> > > > > A couple of suggestions that might help:
> > > > > The number of points in your habitat mask/integration mesh has a big effect on computation time. Check that the extent and resolution of the mask aren't more than is required.
> > > > > You can also try using memory.size() or memory.limit() to increase the amount of RAM R uses.
> > > > > Eric
> > > > >

> > > > > > Hi everyone,
> > > > > > I'm having trouble with my dataset. I think it will take weeks to run. It consist of 1065 capture event, divided int 7 primary and 18 secondary occasions. Additionally I have also D and g0 covariates. I tried to run a null model but after a whole day it aborted and said memory full. I tried collapsing all the secondary occasions into one primary but nothing changed. I tried with ncores=4 but it didn't seem to run better (after 37 minutes didn't ended one run of the null model).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Any other advice, altough I think I have to run separately every session...
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I have a PC, 64 bit, intel I5 quadcore 2.5 GHz, 4 GB RAM.
